@graph.description: Why do traders give back their profits? Three circuits — inflated size, the house-money illusion, no finish line — and the giveback ledger that stops it.
@graph.headline: Why Traders Give Back Their Profits (and How to Stop)

acceptedAnswer.text: Because success itself impairs judgment. Recent wins dominate memory and quietly inflate confidence, your size grows without permission, and with no finish line the session stays open until the market takes the decision back. The biggest losing days usually begin as winning days — the giveback ledger measures exactly how much the afternoon took.

mainEntity.name: Why do my best trading days become my worst days?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not as punishment — as neutrality. Size follows your written plan's risk rule, not the day's mood. After a strong run, the honest check is: would I take this exact size if the day were flat? If not, the position is answering the win, not the setup. The position-sizing article owns the full mechanics.

mainEntity.name: Should I reduce my position size after a winning streak?

acceptedAnswer.text: The illusion that booked profit "isn't really yours yet," so it gets risked more casually than starting capital. Thaler and Johnson named it in 1990 — prior gains make people accept risks they'd otherwise reject. The accounting fix: every rupee in the account is the same rupee. The "house's money" distinction exists only in your head.

mainEntity.name: What is the house money effect in trading?

acceptedAnswer.text: The test: is this trade's size, setup, and stop identical to what your written plan says for a neutral day? Pressing the edge is deliberate — bigger size with the plan's permission. Chasing the feeling is permissionless. If the honest answer is "I wouldn't take this size on a flat day," the position is answering the win, not the setup.
